title: Choosing data structures based on operation requirements (CodeSaathi extension)
learningObjectives: Explain the topic and its C rules.
Trace the example and explain its data or control flow.
Identify edge cases and resource-management requirements.
Apply the concept in a tested C program.

understand.concept: Data-structure selection should begin with required operations, input size, update patterns, ordering needs, memory constraints and failure handling. Arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees and hash tables have different operation costs and implementation complexity.
understand.whyItMatters: The best structure is not universal. Matching the structure to actual operations avoids unnecessary complexity and poor performance.
understand.analogy: Treat each algorithm or resource as a contract whose invariants must remain true after every operation.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace C's formal rules for pointers, object lifetime, complexity or library contracts.

explain.narrative:
Data-structure selection should begin with required operations, input size, update patterns, ordering needs, memory constraints and failure handling. Arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees and hash tables have different operation costs and implementation complexity.

State preconditions, invariants, empty and full cases, ownership and failure behaviour before implementation. Compile with warnings and test normal, boundary and failure paths.

examples.title: Focused C example
examples.explanation: The array supports direct indexed access after bounds validation. A linked list would require traversal to reach the same index, so it would not offer the same access cost.

practise.guidedTask: Choose a structure for a task with frequent random reads and few insertions.
practise.independentTask: Compare array, linked list, queue and hash table choices for a small inventory workload. Justify each choice using operations and constraints.
hints: List the dominant operations before choosing the structure.
Consider memory overhead, locality and implementation risk, not only asymptotic complexity.
Measure a representative workload when performance is important.

questions.prompt: What should be verified before relying on the implementation?
options: Preconditions, invariants, bounds and failure cases.
Only the name of the algorithm.
Whether one input produced a result.
questions.answer: Preconditions, invariants, bounds and failure cases.
questions.explanation: Correctness depends on maintaining the data structure or algorithm contract.

questions.prompt: Which test strategy is most useful?
options: Test empty, boundary and representative operation sequences.
Assume one successful example proves all cases.
questions.answer: Test empty, boundary and representative operation sequences.
questions.explanation: Targeted tests expose defects ordinary examples can miss.
